slideCritiques.evidence: Sparse title slide with only company name, tagline, and 'Seed round · 2026'; no charts, claims, sources, or dense text that would trigger the issue vocabulary.

slideCritiques.purpose: State the pain of online payment fraud and why existing batch tools fail risk teams.
slideCritiques.landsAs: A clean, readable problem statement that fraud costs billions and current tools only catch it after the money moves.
slideCritiques.visibleText:
The problem

Online payment fraud costs companies billions every year.

Existing tools run in batch. By the time they flag a transaction, the money has already moved and the chargeback is inevitable.

Risk teams are stuck reviewing what already happened.

slideCritiques.evidence: The opening claim 'Online payment fraud costs companies billions every year.' is presented with no citation or source.

slideCritiques.purpose: Explain what the product does: real-time inline transaction scoring that returns accept/review/decline before settlement.
slideCritiques.landsAs: A sparse product one-liner that names Sentinel and a latency claim but gives almost no visual or structural sense of the product.
slideCritiques.visibleText:
What we do

Sentinel scores every transaction in under 200 milliseconds, inline, before it settles.

We combine device signals, behavioural features and a low-latency model to give an accept / review / decline decision synchronously.

Team

Our founding team brings together deep, complementary expertise across payments infrastructure, machine learning systems and enterprise go-to-market motions, with a shared history of shipping mission-critical systems at scale in high-regulation environments. Our CEO spent six years at a leading payments company where they led fraud detection initiatives spanning real-time scoring, chargeback mitigation and merchant risk tooling, and worked closely with cross-functional stakeholders across risk, engineering and compliance to deliver measurable reductions in fraud loss rates. Our CTO previously architected distributed low-latency systems and brings a rigorous engineering philosophy focused on reliability, observability and operational excellence. Together the team has built and scaled systems handling significant transaction volumes and has developed a nuanced understanding of the operational, technical and organisational challenges inherent in deploying real-time decisioning infrastructure inside large financial institutions and high-growth fintech companies.

redFlags.summary: Traction is optical: logo soup + unlabeled 40% curve, while ask slide quietly admits only 8 paying
redFlags.whyItMatters: At seed, credible paying demand is the main de-risking signal; inflating with pilots and unscaled charts wastes the meeting and usually means retention/revenue won't hold up.

redFlags.summary: No competition slide in a crowded real-time fraud knife-fight
redFlags.whyItMatters: Fraud scoring has entrenched players (Forter, Sift, Riskified, Stripe Radar, bank in-house). If they can't name who they lose to and why they win, they don't have a wedge.

redFlags.summary: Team slide is an unscannable prose block with no names, prior companies, or proof points
redFlags.whyItMatters: Seed is a bet on founders; if the deck won't even name them or show domain reps, either the team is weak or they're hiding it.

redFlags.summary: Lazy unsourced $50B TAM with '1% = $500M' and no price or bottom-up
redFlags.whyItMatters: Signals they haven't done customer-level math on ACV, attach, or winnable ICP — bad predictor of capital efficiency on a $3M raise.

redFlags.summary: Slide 1 one-liner doesn't match the product the rest of the deck describes
redFlags.whyItMatters: Generic 'AI intelligence platform' framing usually means weak positioning and a deck assembled before they knew what they sell.

caseForNo: Skip this one. Traction is mostly optics: slide 4 leads with “12 design partners” and a 40% WoW curve on an unlabeled axis, while slide 5’s logo grid is footnoted as pilots/trials and slide 8 admits only 8 paying customers today. Market is the usual unsourced $50B → “1% = $500M” on slide 6, team is an unscannable prose block with no names or proof points (slide 7), and there’s no competition slide at all. Real-time fraud scoring is a crowded knife-fight; this deck doesn’t show me why they win it.

plannedProbes.question: Slide 5 titles eight logos 'Our customers' with a footnote that includes pilots and design partners, and slide 8 says eight paying today — are those the same eight, or how many of the logos on five are actually paying, and what are they paying?

The slide 4 curve is labeled volume scored but has no y-axis numbers and no time markers — what was weekly volume at the left edge versus now, over how many weeks, and is that 40% on a base near the eight paying accounts?
There's no competition slide — when a prospect doesn't buy you, who do they go with instead, and can you walk me through the last two deals you lost and why?
Slide 7 is a paragraph with no names — who exactly are the CEO and CTO, where did they work last, and what have either of you shipped in payments or fraud before this?
You're asking for $3M to go from 8 to 100 paying customers in 18 months — what's average ACV, what's the sales motion, and how many of the current eight expanded or churned?

Slide 1 calls this an AI intelligence platform for modern teams, but every other slide is pre-settlement payment scoring under 200ms — why lead with the generic line, and is the product broader than fraud or not?

postureReason: Colleague's decline case matches what I see: traction optics, no competition story, anonymous team, and lazy TAM in a brutal category — I expect to pass unless they demolish the paying-customer and win-rate questions in the first ten minutes.
